newsitem.title: UK: Top Unionist says Britain duplicitous over arms.
newsitem.headline: Top Unionist says Britain duplicitous over arms.

text.p: David Trimble, head of Northern Ireland's most powerful pro-British Unionist party, said on Monday the British government had shown massive duplicity in handling the issue of how guerrillas should surrender their arms.
"We are dealing with duplicity from the Northern Ireland Office on a massive scale," Trimble told BBC Radio Ulster ahead of crunch talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
He suggested that his Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) would not walk out of the Belfast peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland but did not say so explicitly.
Trimble recalled that he had told reporters after talks with Blair at his 10 Downing Street office in London last week that he would continue to take part in the negotiations.
"I said after I came out of Downing Street last Thursday that we are not of a mind to walk out," Trimble recalled.

Asked if he would be prepared to sit face to face with Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish republican IRA guerrilla group fighting to end British rule of the province, he replied: "Well, that is something we don't rule out"
It was Trimble's first public comment since the IRA (Irish Republican Army) declared a ceasefire at the weekend in its 28-year war in a bid to earn Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks in Belfast.
Trimble said that he would be seeking cast-iron reassurances from Blair that the IRA would have to hand over or decommission some weapons as part of the peace process.
"Reassurances are very cheap. What counts is what is down in black and white and what is going to happen," he said.
Such reassurances would "have to be underwritten by the Irish government", so-sponsors of the negotiations, he said.
He said the IRA had called the truce because Sinn Fein had been given to understand by Britain that it would not have to secure the handover of any IRA arms during the talks.
"They (Sinn Fein) interpret it as a guarantee that they don't have to carry out any decommissioning at all," Trimble said.

The UUP says that the Downing Street Declaration, which underpins the four-year Northern Ireland peace process, states that participants to the talks have to give up violence permanently, which means abandoning violence and their arms.
His party and other hardline Unionist groups insist that the IRA agree to hand over arms at the start of the negotiations.
